questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a tariff?
options: A tax on imported goods, which raises their price in the domestic market
A physical limit on the quantity that may be imported
A payment to domestic producers
A ban on trade with a country
questions.why: It raises the domestic price from the world price to the world price plus the tariff.
whyNot: That is a quota.
That is a subsidy.
That is an embargo.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a reason for restriction named in the specification?
options: To protect infant and geriatric industries
To raise the exchange rate
To reduce the national debt
To increase the money supply
questions.why: The six named reasons are infant and geriatric industries, domestic industry and employment, national security, dumping, correcting a current account deficit, and raising revenue.
whyNot: Exchange rate policy is a separate instrument.
Debt reduction is a fiscal matter.
Money supply is monetary policy.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a geriatric industry?
options: A long-established declining industry argued to need protection while it contracts gradually
A new industry too small to compete internationally
An industry employing mainly older workers
An industry producing goods for elderly consumers
questions.why: Protection spreads the adjustment over time so structural unemployment is less concentrated, and it delays inevitable adjustment.
whyNot: That is an infant industry.
The term refers to the industry's stage, not its workforce.
It does not refer to the customers.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a deadweight welfare loss?
options: The loss of welfare caused by an intervention moving the market away from the efficient output
The revenue a government loses when it cuts a tariff
The profit a producer loses when prices fall
The cost of administering a tariff
questions.why: With a tariff it is the part of the consumer loss that becomes neither producer surplus nor government revenue.
whyNot: That is lost tax revenue.
That is a fall in producer surplus.
That is an administrative cost.

questions.stem: Who gains and who loses from a tariff?
options: Domestic producers and the government gain; consumers and importing firms lose
Everyone in the economy gains
Only the government gains and everyone else is unaffected
Consumers gain and producers lose
questions.why: There is also a net deadweight welfare loss, because production shifts to higher-cost domestic producers and some consumption is lost.
whyNot: Consumers pay more and consume less.
Producers gain and consumers lose.
Consumers face higher prices.

questions.stem: Why is a quota generally worse for national welfare than an equivalent tariff?
options: No government revenue is raised, and the gain accrues to whoever holds the import licences
A quota raises the price by more than a tariff always does
A quota cannot be enforced
A quota harms domestic producers
questions.why: The licence holders may be foreign producers, in which case the gain leaves the country entirely.
whyNot: The price effect can be equivalent by construction.
Quotas are enforced at the border.
Domestic producers gain from a quota as from a tariff.

questions.stem: What is distinctive about the burden of a subsidy to domestic producers?
options: The cost falls on taxpayers rather than consumers, and the domestic price does not rise
The cost falls on consumers through higher prices
The cost falls on foreign producers
There is no cost, because it is only a transfer
questions.why: That makes subsidies politically easier and no less distorting, and it means consumers are not the losers here.
whyNot: A subsidy lowers producers' costs without raising the price.
Foreign producers lose market share, not money to the government.
The taxpayer bears a real cost.

questions.stem: Why have non-tariff barriers grown as tariffs have fallen?
options: They are hard to challenge as protectionist when presented as consumer protection
They raise more government revenue than tariffs
The WTO requires members to use them
They are cheaper for exporters to comply with
questions.why: Their cost is compliance and delay rather than a visible tax, so the effect is real and invisible in trade statistics.
whyNot: They raise no revenue at all.
The WTO does not require them.
Compliance and redesign can cost more than a tariff.

questions.stem: Why is protection usually described as regressive between income groups?
options: Tariffs fall most heavily on goods forming a large share of low-income households' spending
Tariffs are levied only on luxury goods
Tariffs are paid entirely by high earners
Tariffs reduce the prices of necessities
questions.why: Food and clothing are the clearest cases. Against that, the jobs protected are often lower-skilled and regionally concentrated, so protection can reduce inequality between regions.
whyNot: Tariffs commonly apply to food and clothing.
The burden falls on all consumers of the taxed good.
Tariffs raise prices.

questions.stem: Why is protecting a domestic industry that produces an input especially costly?
options: It raises costs throughout the economy for every industry that buys from it
It reduces the protected industry's own output
It raises the exchange rate automatically
It prevents the industry from exporting
questions.why: A tariff on steel protects steelmakers and raises costs for every manufacturer that buys steel, and that loss is often larger in aggregate than the gain.
whyNot: The protected industry supplies more, not less.
There is no automatic exchange rate effect.
It may raise the industry's costs of imported inputs, but exporting is not prevented.

questions.stem: Why does the infant industry argument so often fail in practice?
options: Protection removes the pressure to become efficient and the industry lobbies to keep it
Infant industries never reach economies of scale
It is prohibited under WTO rules
Consumers refuse to buy domestically produced goods
questions.why: There is also no reliable mechanism to identify which infant industries would eventually succeed.
whyNot: Some do reach scale; the problem is the incentive to remain protected.
Limited protection is permitted in various forms.
Consumers buy the protected good because the alternative is dearer.

questions.stem: Why is a tariff generally ineffective at correcting a current account deficit?
options: Many imports are inputs, so restriction raises domestic costs, and retaliation reduces exports
Tariffs cannot be applied to services
Current account deficits are always caused by the exchange rate
Tariffs increase the volume of imports
questions.why: It also treats the symptom rather than the cause, which is usually a competitiveness or a savings-investment problem.
whyNot: Barriers apply to services in other forms.
Deficits have several causes.
Tariffs reduce imports; the problem is the side effects.

questions.stem: When can protection be justified, according to the most defensible version of the argument?
options: Where there is an identifiable market failure and a credible plan to remove the protection
Whenever an existing industry faces import competition
Whenever the current account is in deficit
Whenever government revenue needs to rise
questions.why: Where it exists simply to preserve the position of an existing industry, the cost falls on consumers and on the rest of the economy.
whyNot: That describes protection with no exit and no market failure.
Protection treats the symptom of a deficit.
Revenue can be raised in less distorting ways.

questions.stem: What happens to domestic consumption when a tariff is imposed?
options: It falls, because the domestic price has risen
It rises, because domestic output has risen
It is unchanged, because demand is fixed
It rises, because the tariff revenue is returned to consumers
questions.why: Domestic supply rises, consumption falls, and imports are squeezed from both directions.
whyNot: Higher output serves a smaller total market.
Demand responds to price.
Revenue accrues to the government.

questions.stem: Why is preventing dumping a difficult basis for an anti-dumping duty?
options: Proving that a price is below cost is genuinely difficult, and the accusation is easily misused
Dumping has never been observed
The WTO prohibits all anti-dumping measures
Dumping benefits the importing country permanently
questions.why: Anti-dumping actions are widely used as disguised protection against efficient competitors.
whyNot: Predatory pricing does occur.
The WTO permits anti-dumping duties.
Predatory pricing harms consumers once competitors have been driven out.

questions.stem: Why do some governments rely on tariffs for revenue?
options: They are administratively simple to collect where income tax capacity is limited
They raise more revenue than any other tax
They are the only tax permitted by the WTO
They fall entirely on foreign producers
questions.why: The revenue comes from domestic consumers, and it is a regressive way of raising it.
whyNot: Income and consumption taxes usually raise far more.
The WTO does not restrict domestic taxation in this way.
The duty is paid by the importer and passed to consumers.
